title: Part 1, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About what befell Don Quixote's party at the inn

Their tasty meal finished, they saddled up at once, and without any adventure worth mentioning they reached the next day the inn — the object of Sancho Panza's fear and dread; but though he would rather not have gone in, there was no help for it. The landlady, the landlord, their daughter, and Maritornes, when they saw Don Quixote and Sancho coming, went out to welcome them with signs of hearty satisfaction, which Don Quixote received with dignity and gravity; and he told them to make up a better bed for him than the last time. To which the landlady replied that if he paid better than he did the last time, she would give him one fit for a prince. Don Quixote said he would, so they made up a tolerable one for him in the same garret as before; and he lay down at once, being sorely shaken and in want of sleep.
No sooner was the door shut on him than the landlady made for the barber, and seizing him by the beard, said:

"By my faith, you're not going to make a beard of my tail any longer; you must give me back my tail, for it's a shame the way that thing of my husband's is left tossing about on the floor — I mean the comb I used to stick in my good tail."

But for all she tugged at it, the barber would not give it up until the licentiate told him to let her have it, since there was no further need for that stratagem now: he could declare himself and appear in his own character and tell Don Quixote that he had fled to this inn when those thieves the galley slaves robbed him; and if he asked for the princess's squire, they could tell him that she had sent him on ahead to give notice to the people of her kingdom that she was coming, and bringing with her the deliverer of them all. At this the barber cheerfully restored the tail to the landlady, and at the same time they returned all the other items they had borrowed to bring about Don Quixote's deliverance. All the people of the inn were struck with astonishment at the beauty of Dorothea, and even at the comely figure of the shepherd Cardenio. The curate had them get ready such food as there was in the inn, and the landlord, in hope of better payment, served them up a tolerably good dinner. All this time Don Quixote was asleep, and they thought it best not to wake him, since sleeping would now do him more good than eating.

While at dinner, the company consisting of the landlord, his wife, their daughter, Maritornes, and all the travellers, they discussed the strange craze of Don Quixote and the way he had been found; and the landlady told them what had taken place between him and the carrier; and then, looking round to see if Sancho was there, when she saw he wasn't, she gave them the whole story of his blanketing, which they received with no little amusement. But when the curate observed that it was the books of chivalry Don Quixote had read that had turned his brain, the landlord said:

"I can't understand how that can be, for in truth to my mind there's no better reading in the world; I have here two or three of them, with other writings that are the very life — not only of me but of plenty of others. Because when it's harvest time, the reapers flock here on holidays, and there's always one among them who can read, and he takes up one of these books, and we gather round him, thirty or more of us, and stay listening to him with a delight that makes our grey hairs grow young again. At least I can say for myself that when I hear of what furious and terrible blows the knights deliver, the longing seizes me to do the same, and I would like to be hearing about them night and day."

"And so would I," said the landlady, "because I never have a quiet moment in my house except when you're listening to someone reading — for then you're so taken up that for the time being you forget to scold."

"That's true," said Maritornes; "and, faith, I greatly enjoy hearing these things too, for they are very pretty — especially when they describe some lady or other in the arms of her knight under the orange trees, and the duenna keeping watch for them is half dead with envy and fright; all this, I say, is as good as honey."
"And you, what do you think, young lady?" said the curate, turning to the landlord's daughter.

"I really don't know, señor," she said. "I listen too, and to tell the truth, though I don't understand it, I like hearing it. But it's not the blows that my father likes that I like — it's the laments the knights utter when they are separated from their ladies; and indeed they sometimes make me weep with the pity I feel for them."
"Then you would console them if it were for you they wept, young lady?" said Dorothea.

"I don't know what I should do," said the girl. "I only know that there are some of those ladies so cruel that they call their knights tigers and lions and a thousand other foul names; and Jesus! — I don't know what sort of folk they can be, so unfeeling and heartless that, rather than bestow a glance on a worthy man, they leave him to die or go mad. I don't know what's the good of such prudery; if it's for honour's sake, why not marry them? That's all they want."
"Hush, child," said the landlady. "It seems to me you know a great deal about these things, and it's not fitting for girls to know or talk so much."
"Since the gentleman asked me, I couldn't help answering him," said the girl.
"Well then," said the curate, "bring me those books, señor landlord, for I should like to see them."

"With all my heart," said he, and going into his own room he brought out an old valise secured with a little chain, which when opened the curate found to contain three large books and some manuscripts written in a very good hand. The first he opened he found to be _Don Cirongilio of Thrace_; the second, _Don Felixmarte of Hircania_; and the other, the _History of the Great Captain Gonzalo Hernández de Córdoba, with the Life of Diego García de Paredes_.
When the curate read the first two titles he looked over at the barber and said, "We could use my friend's housekeeper and niece here now."
"No," said the barber, "I can do just as well by carrying them out to the yard or to the hearth — and there's a very good fire there."
"What? Your worship would burn my books?" said the landlord.
"Only these two," said the curate, "_Don Cirongilio_ and _Felixmarte_."
"Are my books, then, heretics or phlegmatics, that you want to burn them?" said the landlord.
"Schismatics, you mean, friend," said the barber, "not phlegmatics."

"That's it," said the landlord; "but if you want to burn any, let it be the one about the Great Captain and that Diego García — because I'd rather have a child of mine burnt than either of the other two."

"Brother," said the curate, "those two books are made up of lies and are full of folly and nonsense; but this one about the Great Captain is true history, and contains the deeds of Gonzalo Hernández of Córdoba, who by his many and great achievements earned the title all over the world of the Great Captain — a famous and illustrious name, deserved by him alone. And this Diego García de Paredes was a distinguished knight of the city of Trujillo in Estremadura, a most gallant soldier, of such bodily strength that with one finger he stopped a mill-wheel in full motion; and posted with a two-handed sword at the foot of a bridge he kept a whole vast army from passing across it, and achieved such other exploits that if, instead of his relating them himself with the modesty of a knight and of one writing his own history, some free and impartial writer had recorded them, they would have put in the shade all the deeds of the Hectors, Achilleses, and Rolands."

"Tell that to my father!" said the landlord. "There's a thing to be astonished at — stopping a mill-wheel! By God, your worship should read what I have read of Felixmarte of Hircania, how with one single backstroke he cleft five giants asunder through the middle as if they had been made of bean-pods like the little friars the children make; and another time he attacked a very great and powerful army of more than a million six hundred thousand soldiers, all armed from head to foot, and he routed them all as if they had been flocks of sheep."

"And then, what do you say to the good Cirongilio of Thrace, who was so stout and bold? — as may be seen in the book, where it's told that as he was sailing along a river there came up out of the middle of the water against him a fiery serpent, and as soon as he saw it he flung himself on it and got astride its scaly shoulders, and squeezed its throat with both hands with such force that the serpent, finding it was being throttled, had nothing for it but to let itself sink to the bottom of the river, carrying with it the knight, who would not let go his hold; and when they got down there he found himself among palaces and gardens so beautiful it was a wonder to see; and then the serpent changed itself into an old ancient man, who told him things never heard before. Hold your peace, señor; if you were to hear this you would go mad with delight. A couple of figs for your Great Captain and your Diego García!"
Hearing this, Dorothea said in a whisper to Cardenio, "Our landlord is almost fit to play a second part to Don Quixote."

"I think so," said Cardenio, "because, as he shows, he accepts it as a certainty that everything those books relate happened exactly as it's written down; and the barefoot friars themselves could not persuade him to the contrary."

"But consider, brother," said the curate again, "there never was any Felixmarte of Hircania in the world, nor any Cirongilio of Thrace, or any of the other knights of the same sort that the books of chivalry talk about. The whole thing is the fabrication and invention of idle wits, devised by them for the purpose you describe — of passing the time, as your reapers do when they read. For I swear to you in all seriousness, there never were any such knights in the world, and no such exploits or nonsense ever happened anywhere."

"Try that bone on another dog!" said the landlord. "As if I didn't know how many make five, and where my shoe pinches me. Don't think to feed me with pap, for by God I'm no fool. It's a fine joke for your worship to try to convince me that everything these good books say is nonsense and lies, when they're printed by license of the Lords of the Royal Council — as if they were people who would allow such a load of lies to be printed all together, and so many battles and enchantments that they take away one's senses."

"I have told you, friend," said the curate, "that it's done to divert our idle thoughts; and just as in well-ordered states games of chess, fives, and billiards are allowed for the diversion of those who don't care to work, or aren't obliged to, or can't, so books of this kind are allowed to be printed, on the supposition — which is in fact the truth — that there can be nobody so ignorant as to take any of them for true stories. And if I were allowed now, and the present company wished it, I could say something about the qualities books of chivalry should possess to be good ones, which would be to the advantage and even to the taste of some; but I hope the time will come when I can communicate my ideas to someone who might be able to mend matters. In the meantime, señor landlord, believe what I have said, and take your books and make up your mind about their truth or falsehood; and much good may they do you — and God grant you may not fall lame of the same foot your guest Don Quixote limps on."

"No fear of that," replied the landlord. "I shall not be so mad as to make a knight-errant of myself; I see well enough that things are not now as they used to be in those days when, they say, those famous knights roamed about the world."

Sancho had appeared in the middle of this conversation, and he was very much troubled and downcast by what he heard said about knights-errant being no longer in vogue, and all books of chivalry being folly and lies. He resolved in his heart to wait and see what came of this journey of his master's, and if it didn't turn out as happily as his master expected, he determined to leave him and go back to his wife and children and his ordinary work.

The landlord was carrying away the valise and the books when the curate said to him, "Wait — I want to see what those papers are that are written in such a good hand." The landlord took them out and handed them to him to read, and he saw it was a work of about eight sheets of manuscript, with, in large letters at the beginning, the title _Novel of the Ill-Advised Curiosity_. The curate read three or four lines to himself and said, "I must say the title of this novel doesn't seem bad to me, and I feel an inclination to read it all." To which the landlord replied, "Then your reverence will do well to read it, because I can tell you that some guests who have read it here have been much pleased with it and have begged it from me very earnestly. But I wouldn't give it, meaning to return it to the person who forgot the valise, books, and papers here — since maybe he'll come back here some time or other. And though I know I shall miss the books, faith I mean to return them; for though I am an innkeeper, still I am a Christian."
"You are quite right, friend," said the curate, "but for all that, if the novel pleases me you must let me copy it."
"With all my heart," replied the host.
While they were talking, Cardenio had taken up the novel and begun to read it, and forming the same opinion of it as the curate, he begged him to read it so they might all hear it.
"I would read it," said the curate, "if the time wouldn't be better spent in sleeping."
"It will be rest enough for me," said Dorothea, "to while away the time by listening to some tale, for my spirits are not yet calm enough to let me sleep when it would be seasonable."
"Well then, in that case," said the curate, "I will read it, if only out of curiosity; perhaps it may contain something pleasant."

Master Nicholas added his entreaties to the same effect, and Sancho too; seeing which, and considering that he would give pleasure to all and receive it himself, the curate said, "Well then, everyone attend, for the novel begins like this."
